canonical.name: Smooth cobordism triad for morse theory
canonical.locator: Definition 1.3, printed p.2; local orientation convention from the published boundary definition
canonical.support: Fix boundary identifications and collars as data, including the empty manifold. Reverse the orientation of W when viewing an oriented cobordism backwards.

canonical.name: Morse function adapted to a cobordism
canonical.support: The collar clause makes the positive gradient inward on M0 and outward on M1. Downward fields have opposite signs.

canonical.name: Adapted excellent morse functions exist on compact cobordisms
canonical.support: Patch linear boundary functions and the interior constant 1/2. Apply relative density on the boundaryless interior with a closed collar strip protected. Choose C0 errors below the positive distance from 0 and 1 on the compact perturbation support. The perturbation extends by zero. Critical points lie in a compact interior subset and are isolated, hence finite; separate their values by disjoint constant-near-point bumps, bounded in C1 on transition annuli so no new zeros appear. For n=0 assign distinct values to the finite set.

canonical.name: Adapted cobordism data extend across the boundary
canonical.locator: Lemma 3.2 pp.20–21 and proof of Theorem 3.4 pp.21–23
canonical.support: Glue open collars in the given coordinates and extend the linear functions. Patch the exact Morse fields with negative coordinate fields away from critical points, protecting smaller Morse charts and collars. Positive weighted sums preserve df(X)<0. Flow is used only until boundary hitting or on compact interior slabs; do not assert completeness on W.

canonical.name: Handle decomposition relative to the incoming boundary
canonical.locator: Definition of handle decomposition, PDF p.5
canonical.support: Retain full attaching-region data and boundary identifications; empty M0 starts with the empty manifold.

canonical.name: A framed handle trace admits a compatible morse function
canonical.locator: Theorem 3.12 complete proof pp.30–31; Lemma 3.7 p.26
canonical.support: Use the quadratic q=-|u|^2+|v|^2 on Milnor's trace region |q|<=1, |u|^2|v|^2 bounded. Its non-axis trajectories (e^{-t}u,e^t v) identify the overlap with the product outside the attaching sphere; use q as time. Glue through the supplied framing and check smooth transition maps. At k=0 or n use a ball with a minimum or maximum. Compare to the rounded handle using the earlier local handle-pair result and rounding isotopy.

canonical.name: Morse functions and handle decompositions correspond
canonical.locator: Corollary 2.10 pp.18–19; Lemma 3.7 p.26; Theorems 3.12–3.13 pp.30–32
canonical.support: Cut at regular values in the boundaryless extension. Apply one-handle attachment and regular product bands with lower collars fixed. Conversely concatenate the trace functions on disjoint critical-value windows; normalize collar time derivatives before gluing, then positively rescale the global range. Verify finite empty and endpoint cases.

canonical.name: Dual handle decomposition
canonical.support: Define through the geometric reversed trace, retaining induced framing; attaching sphere dimension becomes n-k-1 and belt sphere dimension becomes k-1.

canonical.name: Handle duality from negating a morse function
canonical.support: In the Morse model 1-f=(1-c)-|v|^2+|u|^2; swap factors and reverse field direction. The outgoing boundary region D^k x S^{n-k-1} becomes the attaching region. For oriented triads reverse W as well. Translation from -f to 1-f changes no differential.

canonical.name: Critical values of disjoint trajectory closures can be interchanged
canonical.support: On the complement of the two critical trajectory sets every orbit crosses the whole slab. Extend a separating boundary cutoff constantly along these orbits, by constants near the compact critical trajectory sets. Prove smoothness there using disjointness, local Morse coordinates, and finite hitting-time continuity. Choose two increasing interval diffeomorphisms fixed near endpoints and translating near the old critical levels; interpolate convexly using the invariant cutoff. Then Xg=(partial G/partial time)Xf<0 and the local Hessians are unchanged. The strictly interior target requirement corrects Nicolaescu's endpoint misprint.

canonical.name: Framed level spheres can be disjoined by a small isotopy
canonical.support: In P x R^{d-p}, Sard applied to the normal projection on Q makes almost every small normal translation disjoint. Realize the translation by a compactly supported normal vector field equal to its constant vector near the path of zero section. Its finite-time flow is the isotopy. Empty spheres need no move.

canonical.name: A level isotopy is realized by changing the gradient like field
canonical.support: Use ascending normalized field Y=X/df(X), hence Yf=1. In its product coordinates push Y forward by (t,z)->(t,h_t(z)), where h_t is stationary near both ends. Multiply by the original negative function df(X) to obtain a downward field matching X near both ends. Ascending transport becomes h composed with old ascending transport; downward transport is its inverse.

canonical.name: Adjacent inverted index critical levels can be separated dynamically
canonical.support: The lower belt spheres have dimension n-k-1, upper attaching spheres l-1; their dimension sum is n+l-k-2<n-1. They are finite disjoint unions with framed neighborhoods. Disjoin them and realize the motion by a field change. Because these are the only two critical levels, any intersection or accumulation connecting the two closed sets would give a connecting orbit; verify this via Morse entry/exit neighborhoods and compact regular-band hitting maps. No global closed-manifold Morse–Smale theorem is invoked.

canonical.name: Morse rearrangement by index
canonical.locator: Theorem 4.8 p.44; Nicolaescu proof of Theorem 2.4.11 pp.60–61
canonical.support: Use adjacent inversions in the finite critical index word. Isolate two adjacent levels, apply dynamic separation and interchange, decreasing the inversion number by one without changing other values. Termination gives index order. Repeated starting values may first be separated by the finite bump construction.

canonical.name: Self indexing morse function existence
canonical.locator: Theorem 4.8, Definition 4.9 p.44; Nicolaescu Definition 2.4.10 and Theorem 2.4.11 pp.58–61
canonical.support: After ordering, successively coalesce adjacent equal-index groups by the group form of rearrangement, first disjoining their level spheres. No trajectories join critical points at equal values. Choose group values with disjoint windows then use a smooth increasing rescaling, fixed in the boundary germs, to attain (k+1)/(n+2). For n=0 all points receive 1/2.

canonical.name: Handles of equal index can be attached on one level
canonical.locator: Extension 4.2 and Theorem 4.8 pp.39,44; simultaneous construction pp.35–36
canonical.support: Use the self-indexing level and simultaneous-attachment theorem on the extended manifold. The disjoint local handles have disjoint transported attaching regions; quotient gluing on disjoint regions commutes. Do not infer independence for arbitrary original attaching maps before the field changes.

canonical.name: Finite cellular approximation for handle models
canonical.locator: Theorem 4.8 with Lemma 4.10 and full proofs pp.349–351
canonical.support: Prove the finite case of cellular approximation: on each source r-cell, remove target cells of dimension >r in decreasing dimension. First use the PL modification in the next proof sentence to miss a point; radially push the punctured target disk to its boundary. For the PL modification, subdivide a cube finely near the preimage of an inner ball in the target open cell, linearly interpolate vertex values in an outer ball, and interpolate with a PL cutoff supported there. Its image near the inner center lies in finitely many r-planes and misses a point when target dimension >r. The half-radius estimate protects the complement. HEP extends each homotopy, fixed on C; only finitely many source and target cells occur.

canonical.name: Finite cell attachments transport across homotopy equivalences
canonical.support: Use a common mapping-cylinder space for u. Attach boundary homotopy cylinders and disk prisms; extend inverse homotopies over each disk by the disk-boundary HEP. Two prism collapses compare the attachments. Explicitly retain the supplied subpair homotopies in the old cylinder, so the conclusion is about pairs and not merely separate total spaces. This is not application of CW HEP to A before A has a CW model.

canonical.name: A handle decomposition gives a relative cw complex
canonical.locator: Milnor Theorem 3.14 pp.32–35, together with Hatcher Theorem 4.8 pp.349–351
canonical.support: First construct a finite CW model for every closed manifold from its finite handles with empty base, using the same following finite induction; that construction does not need a boundary model. This supplies L for M0. After ordering handles, replace each handle by its cell homotopy pair, transport the attaching map to the previous model using the gluing lemma, and cellularly approximate the sphere map. It then lands in the (k-1)-skeleton even if L has higher cells. Attach one k-cell, preserving the comparison of pairs. Arbitrarily ordered presentations are handled by index rearrangement, which preserves all handle counts.

canonical.name: A zero handle joined to a boundary collar is absorbed
canonical.locator: Disk-attachment lemma on PDF p.8; endpoint corollary p.9
canonical.support: Give a direct collar proof: the 0-disk with the joining tube is an n-disk attached along a boundary (n-1)-disk. Straighten the specified foot collar and reparametrize the extended collar back into the old collar; interpolate to the identity at its outer boundary and round compatibly. This special endpoint absorption is proved here, without the later general handle-cancellation theorem. For n=1 the construction just shortens a joined interval.

canonical.name: Connected cobordisms admit presentations without superfluous zero handles
canonical.support: Order handles. Form the finite component graph of the incoming collar and all 0-handles, with 1-handles as edges. Handles of index >=2 cannot join components because their attaching region is connected, so the graph is connected. Grow a tree from the incoming vertex by repeatedly adding an edge to a new vertex; connectivity ensures one exists until all vertices are reached. Attach these tree 1-handles first and absorb each newly joined disk by the local lemma. Transport remaining handles along the resulting diffeomorphisms. n=0 has no such nonempty boundary and the implication is vacuous.

canonical.name: Dual elimination of top index handles
canonical.support: Apply zero-handle elimination to the reversed triad and dualize. This is a separate existence statement; no unproved simultaneous preservation of an already normalized opposite end is asserted.

canonical.name: Product cobordisms have critical point free presentations
canonical.support: Projection has nonzero differential on the interval direction. Conversely use normalized finite-time flow on the compact collar-extended band and its unique inverse. Empty M gives empty W. No assertion is made about a preassigned outgoing parametrization.

canonical.name: Handle decompositions are not canonical
canonical.locator: Theorem 4.8 p.44 and opening of Section 5 p.45
canonical.support: Explain choices and distinguish existence from uniqueness; the later elementary-moves page owns general cancellation and slides.

canonical.name: Relative handle decomposition of a cylinder
canonical.support: Compute df(partial_t)=1 and exhibit identity product coordinates; both boundary circles are retained.

canonical.name: Dual handle presentations of a genus g surface
canonical.locator: Surface handle illustration PDF pp.5–6 and reversal p.9
canonical.support: Specify the standard 4g-gon paired-edge boundary word and thicken its one-vertex graph; verify the resulting band boundary is a single circle before adding the cap. At g=0 this is two disks along their boundary. Do not cite a B-homed surface example as a dependency.

canonical.name: Reordering independent one handles
canonical.support: Both quotients identify disjoint regions of the same disjoint union, so they agree. Choose the two trace functions to put their critical points at either order or the same value; no connecting trajectory is imposed between the independent handles.

canonical.name: Critical levels cannot always be interchanged across a connecting trajectory
canonical.locator: Theorem 4.1 hypothesis pp.37–39; explicit sphere witness is an adaptation
canonical.support: Let X0=-grad_round f. Near north use Morse polar radius r=sqrt((1-z)/2), so X0 has radial coefficient (1+z)r/4; near south use r=sqrt((1+z)/2), with coefficient -(1-z)r/4. Choose a smooth positive multiplier a(z) equal to 8/(1+z) near north and 8/(1-z) near south, interpolated to 1 away from the poles. Then X=aX0 is exactly 2u at the maximum and -2v at the minimum in Cartesian Morse coordinates. Its meridian trajectories have the same images as those of X0, whose height is z(t)=-tanh(t/2); positive bounded rescaling preserves the two infinite-time limits. For Xg<0 and finite s<t, g(p)>=g(gamma(s))>g(gamma(t))>=g(q). The class is nonempty since g=f qualifies.

canonical.name: Empty incoming boundary requires zero handles
canonical.support: Before any 0-handle, a positive-index handle has nonempty attaching region and cannot attach to the empty set. Construct S^n by gluing two n-disks along their full boundary. For n=0 each point itself is a 0-handle.

canonical.name: Self indexing values on a two dimensional cobordism
canonical.support: Compute (k+1)/4 for k=0,1,2 and use the two independent bands to realize repeated index-one critical values. Small disjoint bumps give excellence at the expense of exact self-indexing.
